notes: Long, low calls around 20 kHz with a slight U shape; good calls never go completely flat, unlike the free-tailed bat or silver-haired bat, though distant fragments can look flat. The lowest frequency can vary across a sequence, and power builds toward the centre of the call (Szewczak). Typical values are the means of the two Humboldt State University tables; min and max are those tables' plus and minus one standard deviation. Corcoran and Weller recorded shorter, higher calls from bats flying low along a riparian corridor (median 5.9 ms, peak 25.2 kHz, 28.4 to 24.3 kHz) and found that hoary bats sometimes fly with very quiet 'micro' calls or none at all. The Therya Notes training rows (Mexico) give 11.1 ms, 30.6 to 22.5 kHz, peak 24.5 kHz. The Handbook gives search-approach calls of about 10 ms sweeping from 20 to 17 kHz. Zamora-Gutierrez et al. give much shorter, higher calls (4.3 ms, Fc 28.3 kHz) from partly hand-released bats, which do not agree with the tables and are not used. So the characteristic frequency rests on the Szewczak tables alone. Interval: Corcoran and Weller's median is 190 ms (10th to 90th percentile 113 to 283 ms); Montana's draft guideline gives 250 to 400 ms, sometimes over 500 ms. The range here runs from Corcoran and Weller's 10th percentile to the top of Montana's range. The bat book also lists this species as lasiurus_cinereus.

notes: Also known as Neoromicia nana (the name in Taylor et al.) and as A. nana (the Zambian library). This is a high-frequency bat, near 65 to 70 kHz, not near 43 kHz.

notes: A simple curved FM sweep, sometimes with a knee in the middle and no Myotis-like tail; calls can end in a small arch (Montana calls it a 'dog paw'). Interval: Montana's draft guideline gives 150 to 300 ms and marks it with a question mark. Harmonics are not drawn because no source gives their level.

notes: A constant-frequency call of about 10 ms that ends in a short downward sweep. Gustafson and Schnitzler describe the call as a constant-frequency part making up about seven tenths of the call, followed by a downward sweep of 19 to 21 kHz. The shape follows that: it stays near 118 kHz (Benda et al. measured the start at 118.4 kHz) and drops by about 20 kHz at the end. Duration and peak come from 15 calls of foraging bats or bats flying in roosts in Iran (Benda et al. 2012). Gustafson and Schnitzler give 7 to 10 ms for roosting and flying bats, and Hackett et al. put the constant frequency at about 118 kHz in the Arava valley. The constant frequency differs between individuals and is lower in flight than at rest: resting bats call at 111 to 124 kHz, handled Iranian bats at 121 to 122 kHz, and flying bats at 117 to 118 kHz. The peak range here is from one Iranian sample, so real bats in the region can sit a few kHz either side. Call interval: Benda et al. give a mean gap of 32.3 ms between calls; adding the mean duration gives about 43 ms from call start to call start. This is derived and has one source. End frequency is left out: Benda et al. measured the end 30 dB below the peak (117.1 kHz), which misses the faint final sweep.

notes: A long, flat but sloping call low enough for most people to hear. The three sources that give an average characteristic frequency put it at 11.4 to 12.1 kHz, inside the NSW key's 10 to 15 kHz range; all of these values come from zero-crossing (AnaBat-type) recordings. Pennay et al. warn that harmonics of the Yellow-bellied Sheath-tailed Bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) fall at 10 to 13 kHz and can be mistaken for this species. What varies: just after take-off and while climbing, Herr and Klomp's bats used shorter, steeper sweeps from up to about 27 kHz down to 13 or 14 kHz, at a faster rate. At a crowded dam in South Australia, Kirkley heard calls with a base of 14 to 15 kHz sweeping down from up to 25 kHz, also faster. Pennay notes that some pulses curve up slightly at the end and that odd pulses in a sequence can jump to about 15 kHz; this is not a regular alternation. No source found a regional difference. The only Victorian data are two bats released at their roost at Mt Big Ben. Start frequency min 11 and max 30 kHz are McKenzie and Muir's range across sequences, so some calls are nearly flat; the above-canopy mean in Victoria was 17.1 kHz. Duration is the least settled number: the Victorian released bats gave 10.4 ms on average, against 16.1 ms (11 to 24 ms) and 12 to 23 ms for free-flying bats in Western Australia, so 14 ms is a middle value. Left out because only one source gives them: end frequency (Herr and Klomp, 11.5 kHz), peak frequency (McKenzie and Muir, 11.5 to 14 kHz in spectral analysis), and call interval (Herr and Klomp, about 430 ms above the canopy, without saying whether this is start to start). The shape's last point, 11.5 kHz, is a drawing choice just below the characteristic frequency, where a QCF call's tail sits.

notes: A long narrowband call with most energy in the second harmonic, falling by 1 to 1.5 kHz and ending in a short, steep downward sweep (Ibanez et al. 2002). Typical values are Ibanez et al.'s means for free-flying bats in western Mexico; min and max are their ranges of sequence means. The final frequency is measured 20 dB below the peak, so the steep end sweep reaches lower than drawn. Interval is skewed, with a mode of 115 ms. Supporting values: Orozco-Lugo et al. (Morelos) 14.9 ms, end 37.9 kHz, peak 40.1 kHz, interval 136 ms; Briones-Salas et al. (Oaxaca) 9.0 ms and lowest frequency 40.0 kHz; Zamora-Gutierrez et al. end 39.1 kHz and peak 43.3 kHz. Zamora's calls are shorter (7.9 ms) and include hand-released bats. Start rests on Ibanez alone: Orozco-Lugo gives 39.8 kHz, Zamora 43.7 kHz and Briones-Salas a highest frequency of 45.2 kHz. Orozco-Lugo often saw a short upward sweep at the start, which Ibanez says is generally missing in this species. The Handbook account repeats Ibanez's description, so it is not counted. Bats flying in groups raise their peak frequency (Ibanez et al. 2004).

notes: Two call types alternate: one peaking around 32 kHz and one around 40 kHz, with different curvature. Both keys describe this alternation; sometimes only the lower call is recorded. The whole call band runs from about 45 kHz down to about 29 kHz (Bristol: 46.0 to 28.4 kHz; the Bedfordshire key hears the calls between 30 and 45 kHz). Per-call start and end values are not separately sourced, so the end of the high call is left out and its last shape point (35 kHz) is a drawing choice. The Bristol page gives a power-spectrum peak of 56 kHz, which disagrees with both keys and was not used. Duration 4.3 ms is Obrist's mean over both call types with +/- 1 SD as min and max (calls mostly from released bats). Zingg heard short calls of 2 to 5 ms alternating with quieter calls of about 9 ms, and the Bavarian guide gives under 2 to 3.5 ms for its type A (33 to 36 kHz falling to 30 to 32 kHz) and 2 to 6 ms for its type B (43 to 46 kHz falling to 30 to 35 kHz), so the two calls drawn here have the same length only for lack of per-type means. Interval left out (no source with a number). Calls are short and rapid, like impatient knocking.

notes: Two call types, usually alternating: a short low sweep (type A) and a longer, higher call that bends downward (type B). Numbers are from free-flying bats in Jordan (Benda et al. 2010; 28 A calls and 14 B calls from 3 sequences). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives Sinai values: type A starts 35.9 to 41.9 kHz, peaks 32.4 to 37.2 kHz, ends 25.1 to 31.5 kHz, 2.1 to 4.4 ms; type B starts 43.7 to 46.9 kHz, peaks 38.2 to 45.1 kHz, ends 25.9 to 40.7 kHz. Its type B duration is misprinted ("4-18-8" ms), so duration has one source for type B and is listed as one source for the file. Hackett et al. describe type B in the Arava valley as starting at 42 kHz and ending at 32 kHz. In Jordan some sequences had type A calls only. Call interval is left out: Benda et al. give the gaps between calls (mean 76.8 ms after A calls, 52.6 ms after B calls), not start-to-start times. Type A calls overlap Botta's serotine (Hackett et al.).

notes: A loud, low call that many people can hear. It is a shallow downward sweep that levels off near 19 to 20 kHz. Duration: 11.8 ms on average (6.6 to 15.1 ms) in the southern Carnarvon Basin (McKenzie and Muir 2000, 15 sequences, zero-crossing analysis). The Pilbara study gives 8 to 15 ms (20 bats) and the Kimberley study 10 to 17 ms (10 bats), both measured in spectral view. Characteristic frequency: 19.7 kHz (SD 2.1) in the Pilbara, measured as the peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC). The Kimberley mean is 19.2 kHz, Milne (2002) gives 19.8 kHz (95% interval 16.1 to 23.6 kHz) for the Top End, and the Carnarvon mean minimum frequency is 18.6 kHz. Start frequency rests on the Carnarvon study alone (mean 28 kHz, 20 to 40 kHz). The drawn end at 19.2 kHz is a drawing choice just below the typical characteristic frequency. What varies: Milne's Top End reference calls all came from two bats flying together, which gave pulses that alternate in frequency, mixed with steep 'excited' pulses, so Milne calls the sequences messy. That pattern is likely caused by the bats interacting, so the train is drawn as regular. Milne also says Queensland reference calls are sometimes very flat, just below 20 kHz. The Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 8 wingbeats, so call interval is left out. Similar species: the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) and Lumsden's free-tailed bat (Ozimops lumsdenae) overlap in frequency. The three Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

Bats recorded on release at Sigiriya, Sri Lanka gave shorter calls, 7.7 ms (6.0 to 9.0 ms), sweeping from 39.7 to 17.8 kHz with a peak of 27.6 kHz, and a call interval of 85 ms (75 to 95 ms) (Kusuminda and Yapa 2017). notes: Consecutive search calls alternate between a lower and a higher call, and this is the main field mark. Pennay et al. give the low call 28.5 to 30.5 kHz and the high call 30 to 32.5 kHz in southern NSW, the region next to Victoria. Burgess et al. give an Adelaide example pair of 27.5 and 30 kHz. Linke gives an alternating band of 29 to 33 kHz in the SA Murraylands without saying which call is which, so 29 is read as the bottom of the low call and 33 as the top of the high call. The southern NSW figures were used instead of Pennay's all-NSW range of 25 to 34 kHz (the app's current range), because that range includes Doppler-affected calls at the ends of passes. The Western Australian values from McKenzie and colleagues (30.5, 31.5 and 32.5 kHz) pool both calls and fall inside the same band. No Victorian Fc values were found in an opened source. Pennay found no noticeable variation across NSW, and Law (2003) says the call is consistent across the species' range, so values from other states should hold in Victoria. The Victorian AnaScheme key (Gibson and Lumsden) uses a fitted end frequency of 30.61 to 31.30 kHz in one branch, which is a different measure from Fc. The call is curved: a steep start flattening into a tail that sweeps down a little or ends flat, with no harmonics. Calls are steeper in clutter. In open space the high calls can drop out, leaving only low calls (Pennay only). Pennay also says the high call may be shorter and may start no higher than the low call. That detail has one source, so it only guides the drawing: the high shape starts at 47 kHz instead of 50, and both calls share one duration range. Most likely to be confused with the inland broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens balstoni), which Pennay separates by pulse length: under 10 ms against over 10 ms for this species when cruising. Left out for lack of a second source: start frequency (only McKenzie and Muir give one for search calls, about 50 kHz with a range of 39 to 66 kHz, which sets the drawing's start points), end frequency (only the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives one, 29.6 kHz, from a different recording method; each shape ends just below its call's Fc as a drawing choice), and call interval (only Burgess et al. give one, about 100 to 300 ms and typically 200 to 300 ms, for bats that were probably this species). Peak frequency is left out because the two sources disagree (30.7 to 34.1 kHz against 41.3 kHz) and measured it in different ways. Duration leaves out the handbook's very short calls (printed as 2-7 ms, read as either 2.7 ms or 2 to 7 ms), which look like close-range or hand-release recordings. In montane Victoria and Tasmania some bats end their calls with a pronounced downward droop (Corben and Parnaby 2008); these may be a separate, undescribed species and are not drawn. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: No opened source measured bats in Victoria, so the characteristic frequency (Fc) comes from the regions next to it. The range of 47.5 to 53 kHz covers the two NSW regions that border Victoria in Pennay et al.: 48 to 52 kHz in the Southern region (21 calls) and 47.5 to 53 kHz in the Riverina (9 calls). The South Australian Murray region brochure gives 49 to 52 kHz, inside that range. The typical value of 50.5 kHz is close to the mean (50.3 kHz) of the middle of the Southern NSW range (50), the middle of the Riverina range (50.25), the middle of the SA Murray range (50.5), the Pilbara mean of 50.9 kHz (McKenzie and Bullen, one tagged bat, zero-crossing data) and about 50 kHz in the WA wheatbelt (Bullen and Ford). Sanderson gives about 49 kHz at Belair National Park, SA, for bats that were probably this species. Fc varies by region. Across all of NSW, Pennay et al. give 46.5 to 53 kHz (84 calls). The Tasmanian key (Cawthen) assigns calls of 51.32 to 56 kHz to this species alone and calls of 44.01 to 51.31 kHz to this species or a forest bat (Vespadelus), so Tasmanian bats may call higher than mainland bats. The lower bound of 47.5 kHz sits inside that shared band, and the upper bound of 53 kHz sits inside the band for this species alone. Only that key goes above 53 kHz, so the maximum stays at 53. Call shape: a curved downward sweep that flattens near the Fc and, in search flight, often ends in a short downward tail (Pennay et al.). Cawthen describes the call as L-shaped, sometimes with a slight droop at the end, which could also be read as FM-QCF. McKenzie and Bullen list it as FM to steep FM. The call type stays FM because of the downward tail. The drawing starts at 70 kHz and ends at 48 kHz. Both are drawing choices, because no start or end frequency of search calls is backed by two sources. The flattest part of the drawing sits near 50.5 kHz, the typical Fc, and the last part drops to show the downward tail. Similar species: forest bats that call in the same band. In Victoria these are the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus) and the inland form of the southern forest bat (V. regulus), which calls at 50 kHz or higher along the Murray and can also end in a downward tail. NSW sources also name the eastern forest bat (V. pumilus) and eastern cave bat (V. troughtoni), which overlap with this species at about 49 to 52 kHz. Forest bat calls end with an upturned tail or no tail, while this species often has a downward tail (Pennay et al.; a Sydney consultant report applies the same rule). Pennay et al. say consecutive pulses sometimes alternate a little in shape: every other pulse may start lower, or the bend in the call may step up and down. No source gives two alternating frequencies, so the train is drawn as regular. Pennay et al. also note that hand-released bats of this species take a long time to calm down, and keep giving higher, steeper excited calls before normal search calls. Call length rests on one source so far: McKenzie and Bullen (2009) measured 7 to 8 ms in 63 calls from one tagged bat in the Pilbara, Western Australia. The drawn length, 7.5 ms, is the middle of that range. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives about 3.4 ms for south-west Western Australia, with no sample size, so the two sources disagree; check against Victorian recordings when there are some. McKenzie and Bullen give 7 to 8 ms for one bat in the Pilbara, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 3.4 ms for south-west WA (printed as 3-4, which could also mean 3 to 4 ms). Start, end and peak frequency are left out because only the Handbook gives them: highest frequency 125.8 kHz, lowest 50.4 kHz and peak 63 kHz. These look like close-range full-spectrum measurements, and the 63 kHz peak frequency is a different measure from Fc, so it should not be compared with the Fc range. Call interval is left out because no source gives it in milliseconds; McKenzie and Bullen give one call per one or two wingbeats. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: A curved call: a steep start that bends into a long flat part. Pennay et al. (2004), quoting Reinhold et al. (2001), say the flat part and tail usually take up two thirds or more of the call, and that there is usually no tail, or occasionally an upward one. Duration rests on one source: 6 to 13 ms in the Kimberley (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 12 bats, 131 calls, measured in spectral view), with no mean, so the app uses the middle of the range. Characteristic frequency: Milne (2002) gives 38.4 kHz (95% interval 36.1 to 40.8 kHz) from 33 Top End calls. The Kimberley mean peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC) is 39.4 kHz (SD 1.7), and Pennay et al. give 37 to 40 kHz for Queensland calls (there are no NSW reference calls). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats Milne's figures. No source gives start or end frequency. The drawn start (50 kHz) and end (38 kHz) are drawing choices. Call interval is left out: the Kimberley study gives one call every 1 to 2 wingbeats. Similar species: Milne found the calls identical to those of the little and northern broad-nosed bats (Scotorepens greyii and S. sanborni), which call at 34.6 to 41.4 kHz; only calls below 36.1 kHz can be assigned to Scotorepens. Pennay et al. suggest the long flat part and the lack of an upward tail may help.

notes: Steep sweep that flattens into a tail near 27 to 30 kHz. notes: Calls are curved and often steep, with a long sweep down to the flattest part and no upward hook at the end; now and then the end turns slightly down. That curved shape with a short flat section near the end is why the call type is FM-QCF, although the app and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World call it FM. All numbers come from AnaBat (zero-crossing) recordings, so no source gives a peak frequency. Characteristic frequency is measured only by Pennay et al. (2004): 35 to 39 kHz across NSW (32 calls), and 35.5 to 40.5 kHz in southern NSW (11 calls), the region nearest Victoria, which sets the maximum of 40.5. End frequency is measured only by Jolly: minimum frequency 37.4 kHz, plus or minus 1.3. Because the call has no upward hook, its end sits at or just below the characteristic frequency, and the two sources agree, so both are set to a typical 37 kHz. No source gives 34 kHz, the lower bound the app listed before. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats Pennay's 35 to 39 kHz and is not counted as a separate source. Easily confused with the eastern broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens orion) and the greater broad-nosed bat (Scoteanax rueppellii). Calls below 36.5 kHz are hard to separate from S. rueppellii, and Pennay notes overlap with Scotorepens species at 38 to 39 kHz. Pennay says the call does not appear to vary across NSW, that most reference calls were of poor quality, and that the species' range of calls is not well known. Start frequency is left out because only Jolly gives it (mean maximum 50 kHz). Call length and call interval also rest on Jolly alone, from 33 pulses in a south-eastern Australian call library: duration 4.19 ± 1.65 ms and time since the previous pulse 117 ± 7.0 ms (mean ± standard deviation). The file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly does not say whether the interval runs from start to start. The shape's first point (50 kHz) uses Jolly's mean maximum frequency as a drawing choice; AnaBat often misses the faint start of a call, so the true start may be higher. Neither source describes alternating calls, so one call is drawn. No Xeno-canto recordings of this species were found under any name tried.

notes: A very high, short constant-frequency call that begins and ends with a brief sweep. Duration rests on one source: 3 to 9 ms in the Kimberley (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 12 bats, 42 calls, measured in spectral view), with no mean, so the app uses the middle of the range. Constant frequency: 154.0 kHz (SD 6.4) in the Kimberley. Milne (2002) gives 157 kHz (95% interval 152 to 162 kHz, 4 Top End calls) and says it is much higher than any other bat in the Top End. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 154 to 164 kHz in Papua New Guinea and 163 to 169 kHz in India. The depth of the sweeps at the start and end is a drawing choice: no source measures it. Calls are quiet and very high, so detectors pick them up only at close range, and the species is more often found by harp-trapping (Milne). Call interval is left out: the Kimberley study gives 3 to 9 calls per wingbeat, usually irregularly spaced.

(2015), 34 bats from one cave in Hubei recorded while hanging in a lab. Duration is their mean CF part (6.7 ms) plus their mean FM part (2.6 ms); the end frequency is their mean CF (59.5 kHz) minus their mean FM bandwidth (9.6 kHz). Both rest on that one paper. CF is supported by the Bats of China page (59.2 to 62.5 kHz) and by the Handbook of the Mammals of the World (58 to 62 kHz). Males call about 0.6 kHz higher than females, and females make longer calls (Fu et al. 2015). The Bats of China page describes a brief FM start, but no opened source measures it, so the short rise at the start (from 57.5 kHz) is illustrative; the CF part ends at 72% of the call, from the ratio of the two durations. Calls in flight are shorter than calls of hanging bats (Luo et al. 2022, Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience 16: 920703), so free-flying search calls may be shorter than drawn. No opened source gives a search-flight interval; hanging bats called about 13 times a second.

notes: Duration and peak are the range of individual means for 5 hand-held bats in Kakamega, Kenya (Webala et al.): males called at 132.6 to 134.5 kHz and females at 140.4 to 145.3 kHz, so the drawing (at the middle, 139 kHz) sits between the two. The one Zambian bat started at 132.5 kHz, about 1 kHz below its CF, and ended at 125.8 kHz, about 7.6 kHz below; the drawing uses the same steps below 139 kHz, so its first and last points only show the shape. notes: Long, almost flat calls near 32 to 34 kHz in open air. Numbers are Zingg's medians with quartiles as min and max (N = 134 calls of free-flying bats in three parts of the Swiss Alps). notes: Shorter calls are reverse-J shaped with a distinct inflection; longer calls can be almost flat. Flat calls at 26 kHz or above point to this species, while flat hoary bat calls are lower. notes: Ghost bats use several kinds of call, and the sketch shows only the brief FM calls that bats gave in flight after leaving a roost. Duration: 4.9 ms on average (SD 0.9, 4 to 8 ms) in the Pilbara (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, Table 4, 10 bats, 44 calls). The Kimberley study (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 18 bats, 41 calls) gives 3 to 7 ms. Both were measured in spectral view. Frequency: the mean peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC) is 40.5 kHz (SD 5.5, 29.0 to 55.6 kHz) in the Pilbara and 41.3 kHz (SD 5.8) in the Kimberley, so the calls vary widely in frequency. Shape: both studies describe the calls as complex, often W-, M-, N- or U-shaped in frequency over time, or stepped. The sketch draws a plain downward sweep through the typical frequency because no source gives shape points. Its start (55 kHz) and end (32 kHz) are drawing choices inside the measured range. Other calls, not drawn: bats flying back and forth near a mine entrance in the Pilbara gave prolonged calls of 10 to 50 ms, either constant frequency (mean 26.8 ms, 33.6 to 52.6 kHz) or complex FM (mean 22.9 ms); the authors say these may not be search calls. Ghost bats also make audible chirps and twittering sounds. Spacing between calls is usually irregular; where it is regular it follows the slow wingbeat of about 7 per second. No call interval is given. Milne (2002) says calls are so faint and poorly defined on AnaBat that the species would not be identified that way in a general survey. Similar species: the calls share a band with the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus), long-eared bats (Nyctophilus) and the broad-nosed bats (Scotorepens), and are told apart by their complexity and irregular spacing. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Very short, quiet, steep downward sweeps. Srinivasulu et al. warn that the peak can fall in different harmonics, so values vary between studies. Both the ChiroVox and the Karnataka values come from the one supplement but from different recordings. The times of the middle shape points are illustrative.

notes: Older sources call this bat Mormopterus norfolkensis. Search calls are mostly flat, sometimes with a short first section and a short downward tail, and consecutive calls alternate in frequency. All three sources describe the alternation, and Reardon et al. (2008) say no other Australian free-tailed bat is known to alternate. It may call for several pulses without alternating (Pennay et al. 2004). Duration rests on one source: Reardon et al. say search pulses are usually short, 2 to 4 ms, but that the call is very variable. No mean is given, so the app uses the middle of the range. Frequency: Pennay et al. give a characteristic frequency of 31 to 35 kHz (5 NSW calls; 31 to 33.5 kHz in the north east and 32 to 35 kHz in the Sydney Basin). Reardon et al. give 30 to 35 kHz, and the south-east Queensland key (Reinhold et al. 2001, as quoted by Makeham and Conacher 2007) gives minimum frequencies of 30 to 35 kHz. Pennay et al. and Reinhold et al. share three authors, so they count as one source here, with Reardon et al. as the second. The split into a low and a high call comes from Pennay et al.'s Sydney Basin calls (lower pulses 32 to 33 kHz, higher pulses 34 to 35 kHz), and fits Pennay's 'about 2 kHz' and Reardon's '1 to 4 kHz' between the two. The first section, the tail and their depths are drawing choices: no source gives start or end frequency. No source gives call interval. Similar species: Ride's free-tailed bat (Ozimops ridei) calls in the same band but does not alternate and lacks the short first section and downward tail. Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) also alternates, with a characteristic frequency of 25 to 34 kHz in NSW (Pennay et al.), but its calls are usually curved rather than flat.

notes: No call measurement has two independent sources yet, so this file gives the call type and a rough shape only. Characteristic frequency rests on one source: Bush and Lumsden (2025) give 44 to 50 kHz from unpublished Arthur Rylah Institute reference calls. Conole (1997) gives an average frequency of 48 to 50 kHz, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives a mean frequency of 47.5 to 47.9 kHz and a knee at 48.6 to 49 kHz. Those are different measures from characteristic frequency, and the handbook figures probably come from Conole's work, so they are not counted as a second source. No source found gives call duration, pulse interval, start, end or peak frequency for this subspecies. The shape is a downward sweep that bends into a short tail near 47 to 49 kHz, the band where both the Arthur Rylah Institute figures and Conole's figures sit. The bend comes from the handbook's knee frequency and from characteristic frequency, which by definition marks a flatter part near the end of the call. The shape's start (70 kHz) and end (47 kHz) are placeholders, not measurements. Conole describes this subspecies' calls as steep pulses about 2 to 4 kHz higher than those of the eastern bent-wing bat (M. o. oceanensis, average 43 to 46 kHz). Bush and Lumsden say the two subspecies are hard to tell apart by call and only genetics proves which one it is. The app's earlier range of 43 to 48 kHz is the NSW key's characteristic frequency for the eastern bent-wing bat, not this subspecies. Calls also overlap the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus), southern forest bat (V. regulus) and chocolate wattled bat (Chalinolobus morio), and these are often grouped together as one call type. For the eastern bent-wing bat, the NSW key says call shape and spacing vary within a sequence, while forest bat pulses are evenly spaced; this has not been checked for the southern subspecies. Detection range is thought to be at most 20 to 30 m. Xeno-canto has no Australian bent-wing bat recordings.

notes: Search calls are curved: a steep downward sweep bends into a long, nearly flat section at about 45 to 46 kHz, which often ends in a short downward tail. Call type is FM-QCF rather than plain FM because Pennay et al. (2004), Conole (2000) and Pennay & Lavery (2017) all describe a steep sweep that bends into a long flat section. Similar species: the Large Forest Bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) and the Southern Forest Bat (V. regulus) call in the same frequency band. Pennay et al. describe the call as often ending in a downward tail, and say that calls with no tail or an upward tail cannot be told apart from V. darlingtoni. They also say that pulse shape and the time between calls usually change within a sequence, so the train is uneven. The Southern Bent-wing Bat (M. orianae bassanii) calls higher: Conole (2000) measured a knee frequency of 48.8 kHz and a mean frequency of 47.7 kHz for it, against 45.8 and 45.4 kHz for this subspecies, and the call frequencies of the two subspecies overlap at the extremes where the two populations meet in central Victoria. Near roost exits and in clutter, calls are steep, almost straight and very variable. Characteristic frequency: the 43 to 48 kHz range comes from Pennay et al. alone (72 NSW reference calls; the 2 calls from southern NSW, the region nearest Victoria, were 44 to 47 kHz). Two other sources put the flat section near the typical value of 45.5 kHz. Conole (2000) gives knee and mean frequency, which are related measures but not characteristic frequency. Pennay & Lavery (2017) give a mean characteristic frequency of 44.1 kHz for Solomon Islands bats tentatively named M. cf. oceanensis, which are not the Australian subspecies. Conole reports that calls are the same from Cairns to Orbost in East Gippsland, but neither his measured sample nor Pennay et al.'s includes a Victorian site. A NSW survey report (Specialised Zoological 2023) separated this species from the two forest bats among calls with a characteristic frequency of 40 to 44 kHz, so some calls may fall below 43 kHz. Left out: start, end and peak frequency, because only the Solomon Islands guide gives them (start about 77 kHz, end 42.4 kHz, peak 47.2 kHz). Call length rests on one source so far, and not one from this subspecies: McKenzie and Bullen (2012) measured 5 to 11 ms in 179 calls from 28 bats in the Kimberley, Western Australia, which are the northern subspecies M. orianae orianae. The drawn length, 8 ms, is the middle of that range. The Solomon Islands guide gives a mean of 4.7 ms for bats only tentatively identified as this subspecies, recorded after capture, which may shorten calls. No source gives a number for the time between calls. Drawing choices: the first shape point (70 kHz) lies inside the Solomon Islands start range of 70 to 80 kHz; the knee at 46 kHz follows Conole; the last point (43.5 kHz) shows the downward tail that Pennay et al. and Specialised Zoological describe, and the depth of that tail is a drawing choice. No Xeno-canto recordings of any Australian Miniopterus were found.

notes: A short, steep FM sweep that curves smoothly, often with a well-defined downward tail; some calls show a ledge before the Fc. Peak power usually lasts at least 1 ms (Szewczak). notes: A steep FM sweep with a knee into a shallower body and a short tail; power can sit in several clumps along the call (Szewczak). Longer calls recorded in open air separate it best from other Myotis; short steep calls of all Myotis with a similar Fc look almost the same. Calls over 7 ms with a low lower slope are typical of this species. Some long calls share a feature with the Indiana bat, and in the west short calls are hard to separate from the long-legged myotis. Typical values are the means of the two Humboldt State University tables; min and max are those tables' plus and minus one standard deviation. The Handbook confirms the sweep from about 80 to 40 kHz. Its other numbers could not be used: '45 kHz' does not say which measure it is, and 'calls last 1-5 milliseconds' may be 1 to 5 ms or a misprinted 1.5 ms. So duration, Fc and peak frequency rest on one source. Montana's draft guideline gives the 100 to 200 ms interval. Not checked: Murray, Britzke and Robbins (2001) and Broders et al. (2004) have measured search calls of this species but were not open to read.

notes: A steep, almost straight downward FM sweep with no flat tail, made while flying within about 30 cm of the water to catch prey from the surface. Recordings over water can show regular dips in loudness caused by the echo off the water; these are not part of the call. NSW sources call this species the Southern Myotis, and older papers call it Myotis adversus. It is easily confused with the long-eared bats (Nyctophilus). In the NSW key, Myotis calls start with a steeper slope (over 400 octaves per second) and come less than 75 ms apart; calls 75 to 95 ms apart with a starting slope of 300 to 400 octaves per second cannot be separated from Nyctophilus. Start 72 kHz is the mean of three sources: 70 to 80 kHz (NSW), 80.2 kHz (south-east Queensland) and about 62 kHz (Victoria). End 32 kHz is the mean of 35 to 40 kHz (NSW), 31.2 kHz (Queensland) and about 28 kHz (Victoria). The NSW figures come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, so full-spectrum recordings may show the sweep ending lower. Duration 6 ms is the mean of the three sources and the only value inside both stated ranges: 2 to 6 ms in Victoria (varying with the recording situation), a mean of 5.1 ms in Queensland and 6 to 12 ms in the Kimberley. The maximum of 12 ms comes from the Kimberley only, where calls were measured from frequency-divided recordings. Left out because only one source gives them: peak frequency (35 to 40 kHz, Victoria), characteristic frequency (41.5 kHz, Kimberley) and call interval (the NSW key gives only the under 75 ms identification limit). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World also gives a peak of 80.2 kHz and an interval of 5.1 ms, but these equal its start frequency and call length and look like errors, so they were not used. The NSW key describes a kink near 47 to 50 kHz after which the sweep is less steep; this also rests on one source, so the shape is drawn only slightly curved. Only the Lumsden and Coles abstract is from Victoria, and the NSW reference calls come from the north-east and Sydney, not the south. No Xeno-canto recordings were found.

notes: A steep FM sweep with a pronounced knee; power is focused around the Fc, building gradually and dropping off quickly. Calls usually show only a hint of a tail, and some sequences mix in longer calls (Szewczak). Fc above 47 kHz with a duration over 6 ms helps separate it from the long-legged and little brown myotis; the California myotis has a smoother curve. Typical values are the California Humboldt State University table's means; min and max are its plus and minus one standard deviation. Zamora-Gutierrez et al. (Mexico) give Fc 47.4, start 87.6, end 42.8, peak 52.6 kHz and 3.7 ms, with a knee at 60.7 kHz. The Handbook says calls vary by region: maximum 55.7 to 72.7 kHz and 1.8 to 4.6 ms in Arizona; 60.2 to 78.8 kHz down to 44.4 to 48.6 kHz and 2.2 to 4.2 ms in New Mexico; peak 55.7 kHz with a highest frequency of 87.6 kHz in British Columbia. Both give shorter calls than the table's 5.5 ms, so duration rests on one source. Interval: Montana's draft guideline gives 90 to 175 ms.

notes: Also placed in Laephotis (as L. capensis in the Zambian library). Duration and call interval come from Mutavhatsindi's free-flying bats at De Hoop (419 calls; mean +/- 1 SD); this is the only free-flight source. Bats there were assigned to species by a peak between 35 and 45 kHz, not by capture. Release calls are shorter: 5.1 ms (Schoeman and Jacobs), 3.6 ms (Taylor et al., ANABAT) and 3.5 ms (Zambia). Start, end and characteristic frequencies come from the Zambian library (46 bats, full spectrum). Start is supported by the upper edge of the spectrum at the call start in free flight (70.6 kHz, Mutavhatsindi). End is supported by the ANABAT minimum frequency (37.6 kHz) and Fc by the ANABAT Fc (38.2 kHz) in Taylor et al. Peak is Schoeman and Jacobs' mean +/- 1 SD and has one usable source: the De Hoop value (39.8 kHz) cannot count because the peak was used to pick the calls, and the Zambian peak is higher (46.0 kHz). Free-flying bats at De Hoop called about once every 98 ms; the Zambian release calls came faster (71 ms). Calls are similar to other serotines and house bats near 35 to 40 kHz.

notes: Long, shallow search calls for fast flight in open air, the lowest and longest of the Japanese vespertilionids. The sketch uses Niga et al. (2023): 1163 QCF calls of bats foraging naturally in Asahikawa, Hokkaido, recorded with a microphone array (mean plus or minus one SD). The end point is their minimum frequency, and the start point (23.1 kHz) is that minimum plus their mean bandwidth of 7.8 kHz. Funakoshi (2010) recorded 10 bats at feeding areas in Kyushu: 15.7 ms, end 17.7 kHz, peak 19.5 kHz. Fukui et al. (2004) recorded bats leaving roosts in Hokkaido: 12.0 ms (2.2 to 17.8), start 38.7 kHz, end 20.2 kHz, peak 21.1 kHz. These shorter calls with a steeper start fall outside the ranges of Niga et al., so duration, start and end are each marked as one source; peak frequency agrees. Niga et al. also recorded an FM call type (499 calls, 14.5 ms, peak 23.6 kHz, minimum 19.0 kHz). Calls of bats leaving a roost have several harmonics (Funakoshi 2010). No opened source gives a start-to-start interval for search calls. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World account repeats Fukui et al. (2004), so it is not counted.

notes: Search calls of free-flying bats in open air are almost flat, with a sweep of only about 1.6 kHz. Numbers are Zingg's medians with quartiles as min and max (N = 146). Duration is supported by Obrist (9.3 ms), the Bristol mean (10.9 ms) and the Bavarian guide (qcf 8 to 20 ms); end by Obrist (22.1 +/- 2.1 kHz) and the Bristol minimum (24.7 kHz); peak by Obrist (27.4 +/- 5.1 kHz) and the Portuguese key (23 to 27 kHz). Start rests on one source (HMW's 22 to 26 kHz for QCF calls agrees but does not say whose recordings it is from). Interval 243 ms is Zingg's main mode of 2153 intervals (a second mode at 350 ms); the Bristol mean is 226 ms, HMW gives 220 to 550 ms and the Bedfordshire key 3 to 6 calls a second. Near trees calls get more FM, shorter and higher, like serotine or parti-coloured bat calls. Leisler's bat alternates call frequency less than the noctule, often by only 1 to 2 kHz. The middle shape point is Zingg's frequency at mid-call.

notes: Noctules often alternate a higher and a lower call (a 'chip-chop'); only the Bedfordshire key describes this, with no numbers for the two types, so one call is drawn. Peak can be at or below 20 kHz in the lower calls and up to the mid 20s in the higher ones. The Bristol page and the Raleigh table agree only loosely on duration (19.6 ms against a 4 to 20 ms range), so duration is the least certain number here. Interval 200 ms is the overlap of the 140 to 230 ms table range and the key's 3 to 6 calls a second; the Bristol mean was much slower (336 ms). Start frequency left out (no second source); the shape's first point (24 kHz) is a drawing choice. Leisler's bat is easily confused with it.

notes: A quiet gleaner whose short, steep calls are easily missed on a detector. Duration and peak are Schoeman and Jacobs' means +/- 1 SD for 10 hand-released bats in southern Africa. A single free-flying pass in Israel (Hackett et al.) gave shorter calls, 1.35 +/- 0.13 ms, with the loudest harmonic sweeping from 78 to 63 kHz; those start and end values are used for the drawing and rest on that one pass. Hackett et al. say the energy sits in high harmonics (about equal in two of them), and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World lists peaks at 50, 73, 90 and 113 kHz, so a recording may show several stacked sweeps; the drawing shows only the loudest. No source said by how many dB the other harmonics are quieter, so none are drawn. The Handbook's 73 kHz peak supports the peak value. One unidentified Nycteris bat in Zambia called from 84 to 60 kHz with a 2.1 ms call (Taylor-Boyd et al.). No call interval was found.

Typical values are Zamora-Gutierrez et al.'s means for 8 free-flying sequences from Mexico; min and max are their plus and minus one standard deviation. The Therya Notes training rows (Mexico) agree on peak frequency (20.5 kHz) but give a lower start (23.5 kHz), a higher lowest frequency (18.3 kHz) and a longer duration (12.2 +/- 2.6 ms), so start, end, duration and Fc each rest on Zamora alone. The Szewczak California table pools this species with the pocketed free-tailed bat (Fc 21.1 kHz, 8.6 ms), so its numbers are not used for this species. Pocketed free-tailed bat calls are higher (Zamora Fc 19.5, peak 24.4 kHz) and Eumops perotis calls lower. No call interval was found.

notes: A short, very steep, almost straight downward sweep, like other long-eared bats. Calls are quiet. Duration: 5.6 ms on average (SD 1.0, 3 to 7 ms) in Pilbara mangroves (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, Table 4, 6 bats, 65 calls, partly from Bullen and McKenzie 2002). The Kimberley study (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 11 bats, 136 calls, recorded in the Kimberley) gives 4 to 10 ms. Both were measured in spectral view. Frequency: the Pilbara mean peak frequency of the call (FpeakC) is 51.3 kHz (SD 2.1, 48.2 to 57.6 kHz) and the Kimberley mean is 52.0 kHz (SD 2.7). In a steep call like this the value is close to the middle of the sweep. Milne (2002) gives a characteristic frequency of 47.1 kHz (95% interval 40.1 to 54.1 kHz, 8 Top End calls). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 50 to 52 kHz without a source. No source gives start or end frequency. The drawn start (72 kHz) and end (47 kHz) are drawing choices that keep the sweep inside the app's 35 to 75 kHz range and end near Milne's characteristic frequency. Sequences can include occasional calls outside the species' normal frequency range, which the authors call departure sub-sequences (Pilbara 48 down to 38 kHz, Kimberley 48 to 44 kHz); these are not drawn. Call interval is left out: the studies give one call per wingbeat but no time. Similar species: Milne says its calls cannot be told from other long-eared bats (N. geoffroyi, N. bifax and N. walkeri) on AnaBat, and the Kimberley study could not separate it from N. daedalus. The ghost bat (Macroderma gigas) and the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) use the same band. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Its calls cannot be told apart from those of Gould's Long-eared Bat (N. gouldi) or the Lesser Long-eared Bat (N. geoffroyi). All six experts consulted for a 2015 review of bat recordings from Echuca agreed, and the national survey guidelines and the Arthur Rylah Institute (Victoria) say the same. Calls of the other two species can also end below 35 kHz, so a low end frequency does not identify this species. A 2013 consultant's letter claimed that an end near 35 kHz did, and the 2015 review rejected that claim. A quiet caller with a steep, almost vertical FM sweep, so recordings often catch only part of a call. The numbers come from western NSW, from the NSW call guide (Pennay et al. 2004), which lists this species under its old name N. timoriensis (the national guidelines confirm it is listed as N. timoriensis, south-eastern form), and from Greg Ford's reference calls from southern inland Queensland. No call measurements from Victoria have been published: the Arthur Rylah Institute recorded reference calls at Gunbower in 2024 but has not released values. End frequency: the NSW guide says calls usually end at 31 to 37 kHz, but gives regional averages of 42 and 43 kHz for the same 16 calls, and Ford's calls go as low as 35 kHz. The typical value of 37 kHz is the middle of 31 to 43 kHz. The 43 kHz maximum is an average, so some calls end higher, and the 31 kHz minimum is from the NSW guide alone. Left out: start frequency has only one source (the NSW guide: 60 to 80 kHz, regional averages 70.5 and 71 kHz), so it is not given as a number, but the sketch starts at 70 kHz from that guide. No source gives duration, call interval, peak frequency or characteristic frequency for this species. The guide's mean frequency of 53 kHz is an average over the whole sweep, not the peak or characteristic frequency, so it is not used. The guide's call interval rule for the other long-eared bats (usually more than 95 ms) is not given for this species and is not used.

notes: This call is very hard to tell from the calls of other long-eared bats. Pennay et al. (2004) say it overlaps almost completely with Gould's long-eared bat (N. gouldi), and also with N. bifax and N. timoriensis. The large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) is the other common confusion. Pennay et al. separate the two species by the slope at the start of the call (usually under 300 octaves per second in this species, over 400 in the myotis) and by the pulse interval, which is usually over 95 ms in this species. The bat calls softly, so recordings often show only short fragments of each call, and the start frequency depends on how close the bat is to the microphone. Calls from western NSW are lower and longer than calls from eastern NSW. Social calls recorded in the Riverina are longer than 10 ms and sweep from 45 to 50 kHz down to 20 to 25 kHz; this sketch shows only the search call. All the numbers come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) analysis, so full-spectrum recordings may show a wider sweep and longer calls. Start frequency: the range 65 to 80 kHz is from Pennay et al. and McKenzie and Muir (2000); the mean in Jolly's south-eastern call library is lower, 62 kHz. End frequency is from Pennay et al. (35 to 47 kHz) and Jolly (mean 41 kHz). Characteristic frequency comes only from Western Australian studies (means of 42.5 kHz in the Carnarvon Basin, 47.3 kHz in the Pilbara and 47.4 kHz in the Kimberley); no south-eastern source gives one. The typical value of 45 kHz is the midpoint of the Carnarvon and Pilbara means. Duration: 4 ms is the average of three means (Jolly 2.7 ms, McKenzie and Muir 4.3 ms, Pilbara 5.4 ms). Kimberley bats measured on a spectrogram had calls of 4 to 12 ms; those values are left out of the range. Pulse interval: 90 ms is between Jolly's measured mean of 87 ms and the 95 ms that Pennay et al. give as the usual lower limit. Only Jolly measured the interval, so the file gives no interval range. Peak frequency is left out because only one study measured it (McKenzie and Muir: 40.1 to 49.4 kHz in 22 Western Australian calls). The 47 to 48 kHz peak frequency in the Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats an earlier Western Australian zero-crossing value that is closer to a characteristic frequency. The shape is a steep, almost straight sweep that flattens slightly near 45 kHz and then drops more steeply to the end, as Pennay et al. describe. Xeno-canto has no recordings of any Nyctophilus species (checked November 2026).

notes: The call is a steep, almost vertical FM sweep. Both the NSW call guide (Pennay et al. 2004) and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World say so, and both say it cannot be told apart from other long-eared bats on typical recordings. The NSW guide names the lesser long-eared bat (Nyctophilus geoffroyi), N. bifax and the species it calls N. timoriensis, and says the calls overlap almost completely on standard AnaBat measurements. It separates this species from the large-footed myotis (Myotis macropus) by a pulse interval usually over 95 ms and an initial slope under 300 octaves per second; Myotis is under 75 ms and over 400 octaves per second, and values in between are ambiguous. That 95 ms figure is the guide's threshold for telling the two apart, not a measured interval. Calls are quiet and often appear as short fragments. The bat finds prey mostly by listening for prey sounds and gleans it from foliage or the ground, using echolocation mainly to find its way, so call trains may be sparse or missing in cluttered habitat. The start, end and peak frequencies that follow are left out of the fields. Start frequency is 65 to 80 kHz and end frequency usually 35 to 43 kHz (NSW guide, 56 reference calls). The start is where the visible zero-crossing trace begins, so it depends on how close the bat was, and full-spectrum recordings may start higher. The guide found little difference between NSW regions. In the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria, calls average 68 kHz at the start and 42 kHz at the end (16 calls). The Southern NSW row (67 to 45 kHz) is identical to the same row in the N. geoffroyi account, so it may be a copy error and is not used. Peak frequency is 50 to 53 kHz, mean 51.8 kHz (Handbook of the Mammals of the World, which gives no region or sample size). For call interval there is only the NSW threshold given earlier. Herr et al. (1997) give a mean time between pulses of 142 ms, but its standard deviation (162 ms) is larger than the mean, which suggests gaps from missed pulses were counted, so it is not used. Call length rests on one source: Herr et al. (1997) measured 2.8 ms on average (SD 0.9 ms) from 54 pulses of 13 bats on the western slopes of the Australian Alps near Albury. The range given is the mean plus or minus one SD. Their bats were recorded with AnaBat as they flew off after being released by hand, and such calls can be shorter and steeper than in normal search flight. Figures for N. geoffroyi were not borrowed. The app's current range of 35 to 80 kHz is the NSW guide's lowest end frequency and highest start frequency joined into one span. The Batica page from Bayside, Melbourne repeats it under a 'Characteristic Frequency Range' heading, but it is the whole sweep, not the characteristic frequency, and that page copies the NSW guide's identification notes word for word, so it is not a second source. Herr et al. (1997) give AnaBat means of 62.3 kHz maximum, 39.8 kHz minimum and 46 kHz characteristic frequency (SD 5.9) for this species, but these have not yet been reconciled with the NSW guide, so they are not used as fields. The drawn call starts at 68 kHz and ends at 42 kHz, the Riverina averages, which are single-source values used only to place the line. Its slope eases slightly toward the end. No source mentions alternation, so the regular train is the default for a single call type, not an observation. Xeno-canto has no recordings of any Nyctophilus species.

notes: Check the taxonomy before using this entry. Since Parnaby's 2009 revision, Nyctophilus major is the long-eared bat of south-western Western Australia and southern WA and SA east to the Eyre Peninsula. It is not known from Victoria. The bat once called the greater long-eared bat in Victoria (the south-eastern form of N. timoriensis) is now N. corbeni, which the Victoria list already has as its own entry, so this entry may count one bat twice. The app lists it as Greater long-eared bat; the Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls N. major the Western long-eared bat. The call is a very steep, near-vertical FM sweep. The handbook and the NSW call guide both say long-eared bats (Nyctophilus) cannot easily be told apart by call. Calls are soft, so sequences are often fragmentary. The handbook says it hunts mostly from a perch, finding prey by listening with its large ears, and probably uses echolocation in some cases. No number has two independent sources, so every number is left out. Peak frequency rests on one source: the handbook gives 42 to 47 kHz (mean 44.4 kHz) for WA animals, probably taken from Bullen and McKenzie (2001), which could not be read. No source gave start or end frequency, characteristic frequency, duration or call interval for N. major. The shape's start (70 kHz) and end (40 kHz) are drawing choices, not measurements: a steep, almost straight sweep that passes through the handbook's peak range. For comparison only, the NSW call guide measured the eastern bat now called N. corbeni (a different species) at about 70 to 71 kHz falling to 42 to 43 kHz on average, with an AnaBat mean frequency of 53 kHz. The same guide separates long-eared bats from Myotis by a call interval over 95 ms and a gentler initial slope (under 300 octaves per second); that rule is for the genus and was not measured for this species. Xeno-canto has no recordings of any Nyctophilus.

notes: Very low, narrowband, shallow downward sweeps, among the lowest calls of any South Asian bat. Primary source: Deshpande and Kelkar (2015), free-flying bats (N = 310 in the supplement) near clutter in Karnataka; ranges are mean +/- 1 SD. In open space their calls were longer, 23.1 +/- 2.5 ms, with a 15.1 kHz peak (N = 46 in the supplement). Free-flying bats in Sri Lankan tea estates gave 12.3 ms (7.7 to 18.5 ms), 19.3 to 14.4 kHz and a 16.2 kHz peak, the first records for Sri Lanka (Kusuminda 2024). One hand-released bat in Meghalaya gave 18.5 to 12.4 kHz with a 15.3 kHz peak (Ruedi et al. 2014). The start frequency rests on Deshpande and Kelkar alone; the other sources start lower, near 19 kHz. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World prints the Meghalaya call length as 48 to 60 ms, which does not fit any other record and is not used. The times of the middle shape points are illustrative.

notes: Short downward sweeps with a strong second harmonic. Numbers are from free-flying bats in Jordan (Benda et al. 2010, 66 calls from 9 sequences). Field recordings in Iran (Benda et al. 2012, 10 calls) had shorter calls (3.4 to 4.1 ms) with the end at 22 kHz and peaks of 17 to 30 kHz; hand-released bats in a room called shorter still. Hackett et al. give end frequencies of 18 to 22 kHz in the Arava valley. The second harmonic is drawn 6 dB down because the Handbook of the Mammals of the World reports a study in which it had about half the intensity of the first; -6 dB reads that as half the amplitude (half the power would be -3 dB). The bat usually gleans prey from the ground and calls quietly then, so it is often missed on detectors, but it can also hawk insects in the air with loud calls. Christie's long-eared bat overlaps in every measure; Hackett et al. separate them by end frequency (21 to 25 kHz in Christie's) and by its shorter calls. Call interval: Benda et al. give the gap between calls (72 to 302 ms, mean 142.7); adding the mean duration gives about 150 ms from call start to call start. The Iranian gaps (mean 158 ms) agree. Start frequency has one source, because the Iranian start values are misprinted (mean outside the range).

notes: Older sources call this bat Mormopterus beccarii. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World says Australian bats once placed in M. beccarii are this species, ranging from the Pilbara east across northern Australia, so the Pilbara and Kimberley 'M. beccarii' data are used here. The call is a shallow, curved downward sweep. Duration: 6 to 14 ms in the Kimberley (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 6 bats, 118 calls) and 8 to 13 ms in the Pilbara (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, 6 bats, 85 calls), both measured in spectral view. Neither gives a mean, so the app uses the middle of the range. The southern Carnarvon Basin study (McKenzie and Muir 2000) gives 10.1 ms (6.1 to 13.2 ms) for 'M. beccarii', but the Carnarvon Basin lies south of the range given in the handbook, so that study is not counted. Characteristic frequency: 26.3 kHz (SD 1.6) in the Pilbara, measured as the peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC); 27.6 kHz (SD 1.3) in the Kimberley. Milne (2002) gives 24.3 kHz (95% interval 20.3 to 28.4 kHz), but from 5 Queensland reference calls, because none had been collected in the Top End. The handbook gives a peak frequency of about 24 kHz. No source gives start or end frequency for this species' range. The drawn start (31 kHz) and end (26 kHz) are drawing choices; the start is near the Carnarvon mean maximum frequency of 32.2 kHz. Call interval is left out: the Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 4 wingbeats. Similar species: Milne says it overlaps the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) and needs a discriminant function to separate them, and it just overlaps Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) at 28.2 to 28.4 kHz. The common sheath-tailed bat (Taphozous georgianus) calls in the same band but its calls are flat. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: Older call keys name this species Mormopterus species 4 (long penis form), and the NSW call guide (Pennay et al. 2004) uses that name. Search calls are flat or slightly curved pulses, sometimes ending in a short downward sweep. Consecutive calls keep the same frequency and shape: they do not alternate. Characteristic frequency (Fc) in the NSW reference calls is 26 to 30.5 kHz (30 calls), and 26.5 to 30.5 kHz in the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria. Sanderson (1995) gives about 27 kHz for bats recorded in Belair National Park, South Australia, which he identified from their calls only. The typical Fc of 27.5 kHz is close to the mean of Sanderson's 27 kHz and the middle of the NSW range (28.25 kHz). The maximum of 30.5 kHz comes from the NSW guide only. No Victorian Fc values were found in a source that could be opened. In a 2017 online discussion, G. Ford and T. Reardon say flat pulses can go as low as 24 or 25 kHz, but this is opinion rather than measurement, and Reardon says it of the inland free-tailed bat (Ozimops petersi) as well, so the minimum stays at the NSW guide's 26 kHz. Similar species: Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) calls in the same band, but its calls alternate in frequency or shape and never show a harmonic. Calls between 30 and 30.5 kHz cannot be told apart from the inland free-tailed bat. Upper-harmonic pulses of the yellow-bellied sheath-tailed bat (Saccolaimus flaviventris) can also be confused with this species. An automated key built from northern Victorian reference calls (Gibson & Lumsden 2003) separates this species from Gould's wattled bat in one branch by the lower curvature of its pulses. The NSW guide reports a harmonic of the same shape at about 53 to 60 kHz in some calls, and odd pulses near 40 kHz in the Riverina. The harmonic is not drawn because only the NSW guide reports it and the guide gives no strength for it. Two cautions about the NSW guide: a 2022 consultant report passes on G. Ford's view that the guide's Ozimops reference calls are believed to contain errors, and the guide's text says it has no reference calls from the Southern region while its figure page shows a Southern sequence at about 27 to 30 kHz. Left out because no opened source gives them for this species: call duration, call interval, start frequency, end frequency and peak frequency. Without a call duration the sketch cannot be drawn to scale. Western Australian values for 'Mormopterus planiceps' (McKenzie & Muir 2000; Bullen 2003) are not used, because those bats are now placed in other Ozimops species. The drawn call starts at 31 kHz, an assumed value, drops quickly, and then stays nearly flat to the typical Fc. Ending the drawing at the typical Fc is a drawing choice, because no source gives an end frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Older call keys and papers call this species Mormopterus species 2 or the eastern free-tailed bat. The search call is a flat pulse (QCF on AnaBat recordings) that does not alternate in frequency from one pulse to the next, although the NSW guide says the odd pulse in a sequence can be higher. Characteristic frequency is 28.5 to 31 kHz in the NSW guide (Pennay et al. 2004), from only two reference calls, both from north-east NSW. A key for south-east Queensland and north-east NSW (Reinhold et al. 2001, quoted by Makeham & Conacher 2007) gives 29 to 36 kHz but does not say which frequency it measured. It may be minimum frequency, which in a flat call with no tail is close to the characteristic frequency. The typical 30 kHz is the middle of the 29 to 31 kHz band where the two ranges overlap. The minimum of 28.5 kHz rests on the NSW guide alone, and the maximum of 36 kHz rests on the Reinhold key alone. A consultant report from the Sydney area passes on a remark by G. Ford that the NSW guide's reference calls for this genus may contain errors, so the NSW range is weak. That report treats a call as flat when its initial slope is under 100 octaves per second. An automated key built from reference calls in northern Victoria (Gibson & Lumsden 2003) assigns pulses that end at 30.6 to 31.3 kHz, with low curvature and an almost level start, to this species. That is one step of the key, not the species' full range, but it fits the drawn shape. The same study identified all its reference calls of 'Mormopterus sp. eastern', probably this species, though the article does not say so. Similar species: the east coast free-tailed bat (Micronomus norfolkensis) calls in the same band, but its calls alternate in frequency and have a short first section and a downward sweep at the end, which this species lacks. Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) also calls near 30 kHz but alternates its frequency. In the Victorian key, pulses ending near 31 kHz can also come from Gould's wattled bat or from the free-tailed bat the key calls Mormopterus lp (probably the southern free-tailed bat, Ozimops planiceps), and the key separates this species by its low curvature and level start. Left out because no source gives them for this species: call length, call interval, start frequency, end frequency and peak frequency. Without a call length the sketch cannot be drawn to scale. The drawn call starts at 31.5 kHz, an assumed value for a flat call, and eases down to end at the typical characteristic frequency, because no source reports a tail. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: A steep FM start that changes sharply to a low slope near 47 kHz, then a nearly flat body; calls are consistent through a sequence (Szewczak, who lists it as the western pipistrelle). Its Fc sits just below the California myotis and Yuma myotis, whose calls are much steeper. Typical values are the California Humboldt State University table's means; min and max are its plus and minus one standard deviation. Zamora-Gutierrez et al. (as Pipistrellus hesperus; mostly hand-released and zip-lined bats in Mexico, plus two US sequences) give Fc 44.6, start 66.5, end 43.3, peak 46.5 kHz and 4.8 ms, with a knee at 50.1 kHz. The Handbook account has no echolocation numbers. No call interval was found.

notes: A hockey-stick shape: an almost vertical FM start that bends sharply into a low-slope body below about 47 kHz for most of the call. Calls stay fairly consistent through a sequence, and some show small wiggles (Szewczak). The evening bat has more slope in the body; the eastern red bat is U-shaped with a variable Fc. Typical values are the eastern Humboldt State University table's means; min and max are its plus and minus one standard deviation (full range of durations 3.5 to 12 ms). Zamora-Gutierrez et al. (Canadian recordings donated by B. Fenton and G. Jones) give very similar means: Fc 42.7, start 63.9, end 41.9, peak 44.0 kHz and 7.6 ms, with a knee at 47.7 kHz. The Handbook gives a minimum of 43, maximum of 71.5 and peak of 46 kHz. Its duration is printed '5-6-8 milliseconds' and is not used. No call interval was found.

notes: A narrowband call with most energy in the second harmonic, ending in a short downward sweep. Duration, start and end are Zamora-Gutierrez et al.'s means (36 sequences from Mexico, Panama and French Guiana); min and max are plus and minus one SD. Zamora's frequencies run about 2 kHz higher than the other sources (peak 41.6 +/- 2.4 kHz); the others give Rivera-Parra and Burneo 39.6 kHz (Ecuador), Jung et al. 38.9 kHz (Panama), Rydell et al. 38.6 kHz (Yucatan), and Briones-Salas et al. a highest frequency of 38.8 kHz (Oaxaca). The shape starts at Zamora's start frequency, so the drawn start may be high. Duration is supported by Briones-Salas (6.1 ms) and Rivera-Parra (7.3 ms); Jung (9.3 ms) and MacSwiney (8.8 ms) give longer calls. End is supported by Briones-Salas (lowest 36.6 kHz) and Rivera-Parra (36.3 kHz). Interval is MacSwiney's mean +/- SD for Yucatan (152 +/- 60 ms), available only through Arias-Aguilar; Jung gives 139 and 215 ms. Zamora's recordings were donated partly by MacSwiney, Kalko and Barataud, so they may overlap with those studies. The greater dog-like bat (P. kappleri) calls lower, near 31 kHz.

notes: Search calls are a short FM sweep into a long, nearly flat tail, with the most energy in the tail. Duration, end and peak frequency are Funakoshi's (2010) search-phase calls of 10 bats at feeding areas in Kyushu. Hiryu et al. (2008) recorded wild bats over a rice field near Kyoto: search pulses 9 to 11 ms, terminal frequency 41.2 kHz on average, and an interval of about 100 ms. The interval is that paper's alone, so it is marked as one source; the paper does not say whether it is measured from the start of one pulse to the start of the next. End frequency is also supported by Fukui et al. (2015): their hand-released bats in Korea ended at 44.0 kHz. Peak frequency is supported by the Bats of China page (average 48 kHz) and by the Handbook of the Mammals of the World (43.4 kHz in Hokkaido, 42.9 kHz in Kanagawa). Hand-released and roost-exit calls are much shorter: 5.4 ms in Korea (Fukui et al. 2015) and 3.2 ms in Kyushu (Funakoshi 2010), with peaks near 46 to 48 kHz. No opened source gives a start frequency for search calls; the shape's first point (65 kHz) is the lowest per-bat mean maximum frequency of the Korean hand-release calls and is probably higher than a real search call starts. The Handbook's Kagoshima end frequencies match Funakoshi's site, and its Kyoto values match Hiryu et al., so they are not counted again.

notes: In open space a short sweep into a long, almost flat tail; near clutter or on release the call is much shorter and steeper. Primary source: Devender and Srinivasulu (2022), free-flying bats (N = 79 in the supplement) in open space in Telangana; ranges are mean +/- 1 SD. A larger set of Anabat recordings (N = 184 in the supplement) from Telangana in Srinivasulu et al. (2025) gives a similar peak (34.8 kHz) and duration (7.7 ms) but a lowest frequency of 25.7 +/- 10.4 kHz, below the peak by an implausible amount for this call, so it was not used as the primary. The supplement's full-spectrum Telangana set (35.4 kHz, 9.2 ms, N = 41) agrees with the primary. Shah and Srinivasulu (2020) give 7.7 ms, 46.5 to 36.6 kHz and a 38.1 kHz peak on release in open space in Gujarat; Kusuminda et al. (2017) give a 37.2 kHz peak and 9.0 ms for free-flying bats in open space in Sri Lanka. Shorter, broader calls: Wordley (2014) 59.5 to 35.6 kHz, peak 38.6 kHz, 1.5 to 4.7 ms on release in Tamil Nadu; Chakravarty et al. (2020) 67.0 to 36.9 kHz, peak 41.4 kHz, 4.3 ms on release in Uttarakhand; Raghuram et al. (2014) 102 to 33 kHz, 1.4 ms in a flight tent. Wordley's table prints the same duration mean and SD (2.57 +/- 0.6 ms) for this species and for Horsfield's myotis, so that mean may be a copying error. Overlaps the greater Asiatic yellow bat; Kusuminda (2024) treated the two as one sonotype in Sri Lanka. The times of the middle shape points are illustrative.

notes: FM sweep into a flat tail near 37 to 38 kHz. Numbers are Zingg's medians with his quartiles as min and max (N = 134 calls of free-flying bats, southern Swiss Alps). notes: A mangrove bat. The call is a short steep sweep that turns into a long flat part, an L shape. Milne (2002) says the first section is sometimes very short, so the call looks flat. Characteristic frequency: the Kimberley mean peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC) is 49.0 kHz (SD 1.6). Milne gives a characteristic frequency of 46.6 kHz (95% interval 44.0 to 49.3 kHz) from only 4 Top End calls. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World repeats Milne's figures. No source gives start or end frequency. The drawn start (62 kHz) and end (48.5 kHz) are drawing choices. Call interval is left out: the Kimberley study gives one call every 1 to 3 wingbeats. Similar species: Milne could not separate it on AnaBat from the Cape York pipistrelle (Pipistrellus adamsi) below 45.4 kHz, or from the northern bent-winged bat (Miniopterus orianae orianae) above 46.6 kHz.

notes: A long call with a constant-frequency part, a short upward sweep before it and a downward sweep after it. The drawn call is the second harmonic, which carries most energy. In South America this name covers two cryptic forms: a 53 kHz phonic type (Pteronotus rubiginosus) and a 59 kHz phonic type. In French Guiana and Amapa the constant part is at 53.4 +/- 0.6 kHz (130 bats) or 59.2 +/- 0.7 kHz (127 bats), with no intermediate values (de Thoisy et al. 2014). The drawing uses the Brazilian recordings of Arias-Aguilar et al., which match the 53 kHz type; for the 59 kHz type, read the constant part about 5 kHz higher. Trinidad bats (Pio et al. 2010) peak at 58.2 kHz with calls of 21 ms. Arias-Aguilar et al. give a duty cycle of 31 +/- 11 percent; the call interval is left out because the two sources measured it differently. Start frequency has no measured value; the short upward start is a drawing choice.

notes: A long constant-frequency call with a short upward sweep at the start and a short downward sweep at the end. Numbers are from 82 Vietnamese call sequences (Győrössy et al. 2024), min and max are mean ± 1 SD; the second harmonic carries the most energy. Peak frequency varies a lot between populations: Ith et al. (2015) found 69 to 74 kHz in upper northern Vietnam and southern China, 75 to 84 kHz from northern Thailand to southern Vietnam and Cambodia, 69 to 72 kHz on the peninsula from Chumphon to Songkhla and 77 to 78 kHz from the Thai-Malay border south, and Zhang et al. (2009) found 70 to 88.5 kHz across China. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 71.3 kHz, 29.2 ms in Thailand without naming its source there. Resting bats in eight Chinese colonies called for 30 to 34 ms on average (Guo et al. 2026). The constant part takes up 87% of the call on average (28.4 of 32.8 ms), which sets the shape's knees. Start and end frequency and call interval come from the Vietnamese data only: the Handbook's intervals (59.4 ms Thailand, 45.2 ms Jiangxi, shorter than that call's 46.5 ms duration) look like gaps between calls, not start-to-start, so they are not counted. The Vietnamese data mix free-flying, flight-tent and hand-held calls. No minimum interval is given, because mean minus 1 SD falls below the call length.

No Middle Eastern recordings were found: Benda et al. (2012) note that no echolocation data exist from the Asian part of the range. Duration (mean 53.8 ms) and interval (mean 84.5 ms) are from one source, the handbook's values for Greece, which do not say how the interval was measured. The start and end of the short sweeps are not given by any source, so the first and last shape points only show the shape. Overlaps Mehely's horseshoe bat (about 104 to 112 kHz) and the lesser horseshoe bat (about 101 to 110 kHz in flight in Hungary), so frequency alone does not separate them.

notes: Long constant-frequency part with a very short rise at the start and a short drop at the end. notes: The book's woolly horseshoe bat is the whole species complex. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World now treats mainland bats as R. perniger and keeps R. luctus for the Sunda Islands, and the Vietnamese data (Győrössy et al. 2024) are listed as R. perniger. This sketch uses those 5 Vietnamese call sequences, with min and max from their full range because the sample is small: a very long, low constant-frequency call (the constant part averages 43.9 of 48.3 ms). Chinese bats call at 32.6 to 34.9 kHz (Zhang et al. 2009). Sundaic bats call higher: one bat in Borneo at 38.3 kHz, 64.3 ms (McArthur and Khan 2021, recorded while held), and 42 kHz in Peninsular Malaysia and 42.6 kHz in Singapore (Kingston et al. 2000 and Pottie et al. 2005, as cited by Zhang et al. 2009). The Bornean bat's start (32.1 kHz) and end (27.9 kHz) fall inside the Vietnamese ranges, but its sweeps drop much further below its constant frequency, so start and end are listed as one source. Call interval comes from the Vietnamese data only (start to start; the Bornean interval is not defined); no minimum is given because the shortest intervals overlap the longest calls.

notes: A long constant-frequency call with a short upward sweep at the start and a short downward sweep at the end. Constant frequency: the NSW guide gives a characteristic frequency of 66 to 70 kHz across NSW (36 calls) and 66.5 to 70 kHz in Southern NSW (15 calls), the region next to Victoria. Fullard et al. (2008) measured a mean peak frequency of 68.6 kHz in south-east Queensland, and Robson et al. (2012) give about 68 kHz in Papua New Guinea. The typical 68 kHz is the midpoint of the NSW range. The maximum was 74 kHz before; that came from Coles (2002), a conference abstract that gives 67 to 74 kHz in passing, with no data, place or method. No other source goes above 71 kHz (the Handbook of the Mammals of the World, for north-east Queensland), so the maximum is now the NSW guide's 70 kHz. Call length and interval come from one study only: Fullard et al. (2008) recorded bats flying inside two disused mines in south-east Queensland and one near Cairns, not in open search flight. They measured a mean call length of 52.9 ms and a mean gap of 55.4 ms from the end of one call to the start of the next, so calls start about 105 ms apart (52.9 + 55.4 = 108 ms; from their mean duty cycle of 51.7%, 102 ms). End frequency: Fullard et al. give the terminal sweep as 12.2 kHz below the constant frequency, ending near 56 kHz; Robson et al. give a drop of about 8 kHz (to about 60 kHz) from AnaBat recordings, which tend to lose the faint end of a sweep. No source gives the start frequency of the upward sweep or how long either sweep lasts, so the first shape point (64 kHz) and the times of the second and third points are illustrative. Victorian bats belong to the nominate subspecies, found in eastern NSW and eastern Victoria. The Handbook says Queensland populations seem closer to Rhinolophus achilles than to Victorian bats, so Queensland values may not apply in Victoria. The NSW guide says no other NSW species has a call like this one, and that harmonics with the same shape sometimes show; no source gives their level, so none are drawn. No source reports alternation, so the train is drawn as regular. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

Neither gives a mean, so the app uses the middle of the range. Constant frequency: the Pilbara study measured 112 to 128 kHz, mean 120.2 kHz (SD 3.6). The Handbook of the Mammals of the World also reports this difference (mean 114.6 kHz in northern Australia and 121 kHz in the Pilbara) but does not say where its numbers come from. notes: Tongue clicks, not calls from the larynx. Click length is Yovel et al.'s time-domain measurement (0.076 +/- 0.004 ms, 70 clicks; about 50 to 100 microseconds in their recordings). Older spectrogram measurements, 0.6 to 1.0 ms (Herbert 1985) and 1.0 to 1.5 ms in the field in Iran (Benda et al. 2012), are longer because the spectrogram and echoes smear such short clicks (Yovel et al.). Peak is Benda et al.'s field value (30.7 +/- 3.9 kHz, one bat); Herbert found the most energy at 20 to 40 kHz. The drawing spans Herbert's frequency range, 12 to 70 kHz, as one near-vertical stroke. Clicks come in pairs 15 to 20 ms apart; in free flight a pair is made every 112 to 150 ms (7 to 9 per second), rising to 11 to 16 per second when landing (Herbert). The interval shown is the time between pairs, so each drawn click stands for a pair.

notes: No call measurements from Victoria were found, where the species is a rare summer visitor. The numbers come from New South Wales and Western Australia, plus one reference call of unknown origin that was supplied with the ANABAT system. The search call is long and narrowband: it drops a few kHz and levels off. It is usually slightly curved but can be flat. Flat calls tend to be longer, and curved calls higher and shorter. Many people can hear it. Characteristic frequency is usually 18 to 19 kHz. The NSW guide gives 17.5 to 22.5 kHz, with most calls in an 18 to 20 kHz band, and Western Australian sequences go down to 15 kHz. A sequence sometimes switches to another harmonic for a pulse or two, most often at 28 to 33 kHz, where it can be mistaken for Gould's wattled bat. Odd single pulses can fall anywhere from 15 to 24 kHz. The White-striped Free-tailed Bat is also audible but calls lower, around 11 kHz. In northern Australia the Bare-rumped Sheathtail Bat calls slightly higher and is hard to tell apart, but it does not occur in Victoria. Sources disagree on which harmonic the 18 to 20 kHz band is: the NSW guide treats it as the main harmonic with less common pulses at 9 to 13 kHz, while the Pilbara study puts the fundamental near 16 kHz. Detectors show the 18 to 20 kHz band, so only that band is drawn and no harmonics are listed. Start frequency comes from two zero-crossing measurements of the highest detected frequency (means of 20.8 and 24.1 kHz); full-spectrum recordings may show a higher start. Peak frequency rests on two studies that share a lead author: known bats from the Carnarvon Basin, and Kimberley sequences that were identified with a rule that already required 14 to 21 kHz and pulses longer than 17 ms. The Kimberley values are that paper's averaged peak frequency measured on full-spectrum recordings, not a zero-crossing figure. End frequency is left out because only the ANABAT reference call gives it (18.8 kHz, the same as its characteristic frequency, so that call ends at its flattest part). The shape's last point (18.5 kHz) is set to the typical characteristic frequency. Call interval is left out: the ANABAT reference call gives 221 ms between pulses from a single sequence, and the Western Australian studies say one call is made every 1 to 10 wingbeats, so spacing is irregular and often several hundred ms. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

MacSwiney et al. (2008) give the same peaks for Yucatan (44.5 and 46.8 kHz) with slightly longer calls (9.2 and 8.8 ms) and longer intervals (about 180 ms). The shape uses MacSwiney's lowest and highest frequencies for each call; the slight rise follows Jung's 'qcf up' description and is a drawing choice.
