notes: No numbers are filled in yet, because only one independent source was found. Pennay, Law and Reinhold (2004) measured 12 AnaBat reference calls from NSW. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World account gives the same range and draws on an earlier key by the same authors, so it does not count as a second source. Pennay gives a characteristic frequency of 32 to 36.5 kHz (North East NSW 32 to 36 kHz from 9 calls; Southern NSW 33 to 36 kHz from 3 calls). The knee is usually above 37 kHz, and the call drops more than 3 kHz from the knee to the flat part. The shape is drawn to match these single-source values: a steep sweep that bends at about 38 kHz and flattens to about 34 kHz, with no tail. Its start at 45 kHz is a guess for drawing only. Pennay describes the call as curved, and the handbook as a steep FM/QCF sweep. Most calls have no tail; some end in a short downward tail. No source gives start, end or peak frequency, call length or the gap between calls, or says whether calls alternate, so those fields and the train are left out. Pennay also says the call repertoire is not well known. Most easily confused with the eastern falsistrelle (Falsistrellus tasmaniensis): its calls below 36.5 kHz are hard to tell apart, though this species has the longer drop before the flat part. It also overlaps Scotorepens orion and Scotorepens balstoni. No measurements from Victoria were found, and Southern NSW, the nearest region measured, has only 3 reference calls. The 30 to 38 kHz range the app shows now is wider than any source supports. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Characteristic frequency differs by region. In NSW it is 28 to 34 kHz, and 29 to 34 kHz in the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria, so Victorian calls are most likely in that range. In the southern Carnarvon Basin, Western Australia, it averages 34.3 kHz (range 32.5 to 36.5 kHz), about 4 kHz higher than in NSW, and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World notes that S. balstoni may be more than one species. The typical value of 33 kHz is inside both regional ranges. In open areas the bat may switch to sloped cruise calls at about 28 kHz. The call is a curved FM sweep that flattens near its end. The tail varies: usually it sweeps down or is missing, and sometimes it sweeps up. Similar species: Gould's wattled bat (Chalinolobus gouldii) generally calls at lower frequencies and alternates its call frequency. Both species give cruise calls at 28 to 29 kHz, and above 30 kHz only Gould's wattled bat alternates. The free-tailed bat that the NSW guide calls Mormopterus species 3 has flat calls with an initial slope under 100 octaves per second (OPS), while S. balstoni calls are curved with an initial slope usually over 200 OPS. The greater broad-nosed bat (Scoteanax rueppellii) has its knee above 37 kHz and a pre-characteristic drop of more than 3 kHz. In the Western Australian study, S. balstoni calls overlapped little broad-nosed bat (Scotorepens greyii) calls. Duration: the Western Australian study measured a mean of 4.2 ms (range 3.5 to 4.9 ms) for search and approach calls, and the NSW guide gives cruise calls as usually 7 ms and always under 10 ms. The typical 5.5 ms is the midpoint of those two values, and each flight phase has only one source. Left out because only one source gives them: peak frequency, 34.1 to 38.7 kHz (7 calls, Western Australia); start frequency, mean 65.8 kHz and range 57 to 74 kHz (Western Australia); and the knee, the bend between the steep sweep and the flat tail, which the NSW guide puts below 37 kHz and usually at 31 to 33 kHz. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World and Wikipedia list the Western Australian peak frequency range as characteristic frequency. No source gives call interval or end frequency. The drawn call starts at 60 kHz, inside the Western Australian start range but below its mean because NSW calls are lower, and ends at the typical characteristic frequency. The regular call train rests on the NSW guide alone: the guide separates Gould's wattled bat from this species by alternation, which implies that S. balstoni does not alternate. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: A curved call: a steep sweep that flattens into a short flat part near its end, with no tail or a short downward tail. The bat book lists it as FM; both sources describe a sweep that flattens, so it is FM-QCF here. Its calls overlap with, and are often impossible to tell from, the Eastern Falsistrelle (Falsistrellus tasmaniensis) and the Greater Broad-nosed Bat (Scoteanax rueppellii). The Inland Broad-nosed Bat (Scotorepens balstoni) calls a little lower, at 28 to 34 kHz. Only one independent source gives numbers: Pennay, Law and Reinhold (2004), from 21 NSW AnaBat reference calls. It gives a characteristic frequency of 34.5 to 37.5 kHz across NSW and 34.5 to 37 kHz in Southern NSW, the region nearest Victoria. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 34 to 38 kHz but takes it from Pennay, so it is not a second source. For that reason the characteristic frequency is left out as a field, and the shape's end at 36 kHz rests on Pennay alone. No Victorian measurements were found. Pennay says the knee is usually above 38 kHz, but the same guide's Greater Broad-nosed Bat account implies a lower knee, so the knee is uncertain. No source gives start frequency, end frequency, peak frequency, call length or call interval. The shape's first point (48 kHz) is a placeholder for drawing, not a measured value. No source mentions alternating calls, so the train is drawn as regular. One consultant report gives 28 to 36 kHz, which looks like a mix-up with the Inland Broad-nosed Bat and was not used. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this genus.

notes: Duration, start, end and interval come from Mutavhatsindi's free-flying bats at De Hoop (101 calls; mean +/- 1 SD). Start and end are the peak frequencies at the start and at the end of the call in that study. Bats there were assigned to species by a peak between 18 and 25 kHz, so that study's overall peak (22.6 kHz) cannot count as support; peak is Schoeman and Jacobs' mean +/- 1 SD from hand-released bats. End is supported by the ANABAT minimum frequency in Taylor et al. (21.6 kHz). Their ANABAT maximum frequency (28.3 kHz) falls in the start range but is a different measure, so start has one source. Duration is supported by Schoeman and Jacobs (9.6 ms); ANABAT release calls in Taylor et al. are shorter (7.2 ms). Free-flying bats called about three times a second; interval has one source. Long calls with a peak of 25 kHz or more at De Hoop were treated as Roberts's flat-headed bat (Sauromys petrophilus) and left out. No Middle Eastern or Asian measurements were found.

notes: Open-air search calls are long and shallow, near 25 to 28 kHz, with a short downward start and often a small upswing into the call and a downswing out of it (Szewczak). Bats also shift frequency away from other bats calling nearby (Gillam et al.). Easily confused with the big brown bat, silver-haired bat and hoary bat. The Therya Notes training rows (Mexico) give 12.0 ms, 30.2 to 23.3 kHz and peak 25.5 kHz. The Handbook gives a QCF call averaging about 26 kHz. notes: Long, low, narrow search calls, often audible, with long gaps between calls. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World's peak of 13.5 to 15.3 kHz matches Funakoshi's range, so it is not counted separately. Social calls of unknown bats overlap this band, so check the call shape and the whole sequence, not only the frequency.

notes: A long, almost flat call near 24 kHz. Milne (2002) describes it as long and straight or slightly curved, and almost horizontal, which sets it apart from other Top End species. Bats that have just been released by hand give curved calls at first, which Milne says are not typical of search flight. Duration: 13.3 ms on average (9.5 to 17.3 ms) in the southern Carnarvon Basin (McKenzie and Muir 2000, 6 sequences, zero-crossing analysis). The Kimberley study (McKenzie and Bullen 2012, 15 bats, 138 calls) gives 10 to 20 ms, measured in spectral view. The Pilbara table (McKenzie and Bullen 2009) credits this species' column to McKenzie and Muir, so it is not counted again. Characteristic frequency: Milne gives 24.1 kHz (95% interval 23.3 to 24.9 kHz, 6 Top End calls). The Kimberley mean peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC, a zero-crossing count) is 24.8 kHz (SD 0.6), and the Carnarvon mean minimum frequency is 23.8 kHz (23.0 to 24.5). Start frequency rests on the Carnarvon study alone: 24.9 kHz on average, 24.0 to 26.5 kHz, so the call drops only about 1 kHz. The drawn end (24.0 kHz) is close to the Carnarvon minimum frequency and is a drawing choice. The three studies come from two research groups: the two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions. Call interval is left out. The Western Australian studies give one call every 1 to 7 wingbeats, so spacing varies. Similar species: Hill's sheath-tailed bat (T. hilli) could not be told apart in the Pilbara, and the Arnhem sheath-tailed bat (T. kapalgensis) in the Top End uses much shorter calls (under 8 ms). Beccari's or Lumsden's free-tailed bat (Ozimops lumsdenae) overlaps in frequency but its calls are curved. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives a peak of 25 kHz without a source.

notes: A curved FM sweep that flattens into its lowest, flattest part near the end of the call, and usually ends with a short upward sweep. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls the call FM/QCF. Calls in a sequence keep the same frequency, with no alternation. The flat part is drawn at 45 kHz because both frequency sources put it there: the NSW guide gives a characteristic frequency of 44.5 to 45.5 kHz for the only calls confirmed by a museum specimen (2 calls from the Riverina, the NSW region next to Victoria), and Bullen and McKenzie (2019) give a peak frequency of typically 44 to 47 kHz. These are different measures with one source each, so neither is given as a number in this file. The NSW guide's wider range of 39 to 46 kHz (23 calls) comes mostly from 21 calls recorded at Nanya in far western NSW, which may be from the little forest bat (V. vulturnus) or from both species. The guide also lists the Riverina among regions with no reference calls, which contradicts its own Riverina figure, and labels its example Riverina call with a question mark. Bullen and McKenzie do not say where their calls were recorded. No source gives start or end frequency, call duration or call interval, so these are left out. The drawn start of 60 kHz, and the end of 46.5 kHz that shows the upward sweep, are drawing choices, not measurements. Similar species: the little forest bat overlaps in frequency (47 to 48 kHz in the north west of NSW, 43 to 50 kHz in the Riverina), and the NSW guide says this species is hard to identify in the field. The little pied bat (Chalinolobus picatus) calls at similar frequencies but alternates its call frequency. When looking for the bristle-faced free-tailed bat (Setirostris eleryi), Bullen and McKenzie left out sequences with every call above 43 kHz, because those overlap this species in frequency and call shape. The regular call train and the upward tail rest on the NSW guide alone. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species or of any other Vespadelus.

notes: This sketch uses values from southern NSW and the NSW Riverina, next to Victoria, and from the South Australian Murraylands. The characteristic frequency changes gradually across the range: in NSW it falls from the north-east to the south-east and rises again further west (Pennay et al.). Pennay et al. give 40 to 44 kHz for most of southern NSW, 38 to 40 kHz in the far south-east corner next to East Gippsland, and 40 to 44 kHz in the Riverina (5 calls), with a shift to higher frequencies towards the west. The sample size printed after the south-east corner figure (17 calls) may refer to the whole southern region. Linke gives 40 to 42 kHz in the South Australian Murraylands without naming the measure. The minimum of 38 kHz rests on Pennay's south-east corner figure alone. The maximum of 44 kHz is the top of the southern NSW and Riverina ranges. The typical value of 42 kHz is the middle of those ranges, the top of Linke's range, and close to the mean minimum frequency (41.9 kHz) and fitted curve minimum (42.1 kHz) that Jolly measured. Over all of NSW the range is 38 to 46 kHz (89 calls), the range the bat book gives, and it reaches 43 to 48 kHz near the Queensland border. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World gives 38 to 48 kHz, which repeats the NSW data. Gibson and Lumsden say the range is much wider in northern Victoria than further south, filling the gap between 40 and 50 kHz, but they give no figure, so calls above 44 kHz from northern Victoria may still be this species. Their northern Victorian key could name the species for fewer than 40% of its reference calls; the rest went to species groups or unknowns. Call shape: a curved downward sweep that flattens into a flat section near the characteristic frequency. Pennay et al. say the flat section is often long and the tail is absent or turns up, with some down-turned tails in the Riverina. The Handbook calls it a broad FM/QCF call. So the call type is FM-QCF rather than the plain FM the app listed, and the drawing bends early and has a long flat tail. The drawing starts at 54 kHz, the mean maximum frequency from Jolly, the only source for start frequency. That figure comes from zero-crossing recordings, so the start seen on full-spectrum recordings is probably higher. The drawing ends flat at 42 kHz, the typical characteristic frequency, because no second source gives an end frequency. Pennay et al. say pulses in a sequence are even and consecutive, so the train is drawn as regular; this rests on that one source. Similar species: the southern forest bat (Vespadelus regulus) calls in the same band in southern NSW and Victoria. In southern NSW its flat section is usually shorter than 1.8 ms, but the large forest bat can also have a short flat section (Pennay et al.). Lentini et al. pooled the two species as one 40 to 45 kHz group in the NSW wheat-sheep belt, and Linke gives the southern forest bat as about 42 kHz in the same survey without saying how the two were separated. In Jolly's table the large forest bat has a lower minimum frequency (41.9 kHz) than the southern forest bat (44.2 kHz) and the little forest bat, Vespadelus vulturnus (45.0 kHz). Bent-wing bats (Miniopterus) call in a similar range, but their pulse shape and spacing change within a sequence, while large forest bat pulses are even and consecutive and lack a downward tail (Pennay et al.). Start and end frequency are left out because only one source gives them. Call length and call interval rest on that one source (Jolly) until a second is found; the file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly measured 433 pulses pooled from whole files in the South-eastern Australian bat call library at Charles Sturt University: duration 4.76 ± 1.63 ms, time since the previous pulse 97 ± 13 ms, maximum frequency 53.8 ± 8.0 kHz and minimum frequency 41.9 ± 1.8 kHz (mean ± standard deviation). A review in the same newsletter issue notes that some of the large forest bat files may have needed calibrating. No source gives peak frequency. The Pennay et al. and Jolly figures come from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, and Linke names neither the measure nor the recording mode, so none is given as peak frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species or genus.

notes: A short, steep downward sweep that bends into a flatter end. Duration: 4.5 ms on average (3.2 to 6.0 ms) in the southern Carnarvon Basin (McKenzie and Muir 2000, 9 sequences, zero-crossing analysis). The Pilbara study (McKenzie and Bullen 2009, 18 bats, 77 calls) gives 4 to 8 ms, measured in spectral view. Characteristic frequency: 55.8 kHz (SD 1.8) in the Pilbara, measured as the peak frequency of the main part of the call (FpeakC). The Carnarvon mean minimum frequency is lower, 53.4 kHz (51.0 to 56.5 kHz). Milne (2002) and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World both give about 53 kHz, but Milne takes it from McKenzie and Muir, so neither is counted as another source. Start frequency rests on the Carnarvon study alone: mean 78.3 kHz, 64 to 99 kHz. The drawn end (55 kHz) is a drawing choice just below the typical characteristic frequency. Call interval is left out: the Pilbara study gives one call per wingbeat but no time. The species is absent from the Kimberley study because it reaches only the dry southern edge of the Kimberley. The two Western Australian papers share authors and methods but used different bats in different regions.

notes: This sketch shows the southern form of the call, which is the form heard across southern and eastern Victoria. Bats in northern Victoria call about 10 kHz higher. Along the Murray River west of Albury, the characteristic frequency is 50 to 55 kHz in the NSW Riverina (Pennay et al., 38 calls) and 51 to 57 kHz in northern Victoria (Gibson and Lumsden). Riverina calls often end in a long downward tail and rarely go below 50 kHz. Lentini et al. and the Handbook of the Mammals of the World give 54 to 55 kHz for this high form, but both repeat the NSW data of Law et al. (2002), and the Handbook labels it southern NSW. Pennay et al. report an abrupt change near Albury: bats at Albury, Hume Dam and further west call at 50 kHz or higher, while bats at Tabletop (30 km north of Albury) and Tumbarumba call at 40 to 44 kHz. A call near 52 kHz from the Murray plains can still be this species. Together the two forms cover 39 to 57 kHz. Characteristic frequency of the southern form: 40 to 44.5 kHz in southern NSW (Pennay et al., 29 calls); 39 to 47 kHz in southern Victoria (Gibson and Lumsden, quoting Duffy et al. 2000, with the measure not named); 41.6 to 44 kHz in Tasmania (Cawthen, in a key step that does not separate this species from the large forest bat); and about 42 kHz in two South Australian surveys (Linke, and Sanderson, whose identification was tentative). The minimum and maximum cover the southern NSW and southern Victoria ranges. The typical value of 42 kHz is the middle of the southern NSW range and matches the South Australian figures. The Handbook gives 40 to 43 kHz for south-eastern NSW, which repeats the NSW data. Call shape: a steep downward sweep that bends into a short flat section near the characteristic frequency. Pennay et al. describe the call as curved, Cawthen as L-shaped, and the Handbook as steep FM/QCF, so the call type is FM-QCF. In southern NSW the flat section is usually shorter than 1.8 ms (Pennay et al.), so the drawing bends late and has a short tail. The tail varies and can turn up or down. The drawing ends flat at 42 kHz, the typical characteristic frequency, because no second source gives an end frequency. The drawing starts at 60 kHz, close to the mean maximum frequency of 60.7 kHz measured by Jolly, which is the only source for start frequency. Similar species: the large forest bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) calls in the same band, and the Tasmanian key (Cawthen) and the NSW farmland key used by Lentini et al. group the two species together. Pennay et al. say this species usually has a shorter flat section, but large forest bat calls can be short too. Jolly found almost no difference between the calls of this species and the little forest bat (Vespadelus vulturnus): a discriminant analysis in that study classed 77% of southern forest bat pulses correctly. Bent-wing bats (Miniopterus) call in a similar range, but their pulse shape and spacing change within a sequence, while southern forest bat pulses are even and consistent (Pennay et al.). In the Riverina the high form overlaps the chocolate wattled bat (Chalinolobus morio), which tends to alternate its pulse shape. Start and end frequency are left out because only one source gives them. Call length and call interval rest on that one source (Jolly) until a second is found; the file uses the mean as the typical value and one standard deviation either side as min and max. Jolly measured 162 pulses from the South-eastern Australian bat call library at Charles Sturt University, with the recording locality not stated: duration 3.84 ± 1.07 ms, time since the previous pulse 87 ± 7.3 ms, maximum frequency 60.7 ± 8.6 kHz and minimum frequency 44.2 ± 1.4 kHz (mean ± standard deviation). The regular call train rests on Pennay et al. alone. No source gives peak frequency from full-spectrum recordings. All frequencies here are characteristic, minimum or maximum frequencies measured from zero-crossing (AnaBat) recordings, so none is given as peak frequency. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Characteristic frequency (Fc) differs between regions, sometimes abruptly. The Fc range in this file covers Victoria and the NSW regions next to it. Pennay et al. give 44 to 47 kHz for southern NSW (from Eden west across the Great Dividing Range to the South West Slopes, next to eastern and north-eastern Victoria) and 44.5 to 51 kHz for the Riverina (next to northern Victoria). Kutt's AnaBat II readings of bats released in East Gippsland, Victoria, are 44.5 and 46 kHz in free flight. These are cursor readings, not formal Fc measurements. Jolly measured a mean minimum frequency of 45 kHz in a south-eastern Australian call library, which matches a flat part near 45 to 46 kHz. The typical Fc of 46 kHz is inside both NSW ranges and equal to the higher of Kutt's two free-flight readings (44.5 and 46 kHz). The upper limit of the app's current range (45 to 53 kHz) matches the values for coastal NSW north of Narooma (49 to 53.5 kHz) and the Sydney Basin (48.5 to 53 kHz), and neither region is in Victoria. Across all of NSW, Fc is 42.5 to 53 kHz. A Landcare survey in the South Australian Murraylands gives 48 to 55 kHz and does not say which frequency it measured. Gibson and Lumsden report that in northern Victoria, where the southern forest bat (Vespadelus regulus) calls at 51 to 57 kHz, the calls of little forest bats and large forest bats cover a wider frequency range, including the 40 to 50 kHz band. They give no figures, so calls from northern Victoria may fall outside this file's range. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World describes three distinct call types across the species' range and says they may belong to separate species. Call shape: a curved FM sweep that flattens near its end, almost always followed by a prominent upward-sweeping tail (Pennay et al.). The tail is the main field mark, but no source gives its height, so the drawing ends at the typical Fc without a tail. Calls are flatter in open areas. Fc can drift by up to 4 to 5 kHz within one sequence, which Pennay et al. put down to Doppler shift as the bat circles. Above the canopy, Kutt recorded paired pulses (a short steep pulse, then a longer shallow pulse) about 153 ms apart; the drawing does not show these. Similar species: on AnaBat measurements, southern forest bat calls are nearly identical to little forest bat calls (Jolly), and two of Jolly's little forest bat files came from females that may have been southern forest bats. Away from the coast, calls below 44 kHz can overlap with the large forest bat (Vespadelus darlingtoni) (Pennay et al.). Bent-winged bats (Miniopterus) give uneven consecutive pulses, while little forest bat pulses are even in shape and spacing. Duration: Jolly's mean over 362 pulses is 3.45 ms (standard deviation 1.28 ms). Kutt's readings for a bat on a harness (3.18 ms) and in a small room (4.92 ms) fall on either side of that mean, so the typical duration is 3.5 ms and the minimum (2.2 ms) is Jolly's mean minus one standard deviation, rounded. Kutt's two free-flight readings, 7.67 and 9.56 ms, are much longer than Jolly's mean. Each is one pulse picked with the AnaBat cursor, so the maximum of 9.6 ms comes from a single pulse. Interval: Jolly's mean is 90 ms (standard deviation 14.5 ms), and Kutt's free-flight and harness readings are 89.5 and 86.6 ms. The minimum and maximum are Jolly's mean minus and plus one standard deviation. Neither source says whether its interval runs from the start of one call to the start of the next. Jolly divided gaps of two or three times the median gap to allow for missed pulses, and dropped longer gaps. Kutt's 51.1 ms interval (bat in a small room) and 153 ms interval (paired pulses above the canopy) are left out because neither is search flight. The regular call train is based on Pennay et al. alone: they describe consecutive pulses as even, and no source discusses alternation. Left out: start frequency, because only Jolly gives one (mean 63 kHz, file means 58.4 to 67.5 kHz); the drawing starts at 63 kHz. End frequency, because only Jolly gives a related value: a minimum frequency of about 45 kHz, which for a call with an upward tail is the bottom of the curve, not its end. Gonsalves et al. (2013) give an end frequency of 50 to 53 kHz, but for coastal NSW bats, and Law, a co-author of Pennay et al., is one of its authors. Peak frequency, because no source gives it; Fc is a different measure and is not used in its place. The drawn curve averages about 50 kHz, close to Jolly's mean frequency of 50.1 kHz. The call type is FM because Pennay et al. and Kutt both describe a curved FM call; the Handbook of the Mammals of the World calls it FM/QCF. Xeno-canto has no recordings of this species.

notes: Shallow FM into a flat tail near 23 to 25 kHz. Unlike the noctule, it does not alternate high and low calls in a regular pattern (Zingg never saw it; the Bavarian guide agrees). Numbers are Zingg's medians with quartiles as min and max (N = 159 calls of free-flying bats). Duration is supported by Obrist (15.0 +/- 3.8 ms) and the Bavarian guide (cf and qcf calls 12 to 26 ms); start by Obrist's highest frequency (35.8 +/- 10.5 kHz); peak by Obrist (24.6 kHz) and HMW (22 to 27 kHz). End rests on one source; the Bavarian characteristic frequency (21 to 25 kHz) agrees and Obrist's lowest frequency is lower (20.2 kHz). High-flying bats give calls over 20 ms long. Interval is the 200 to 300 ms band that held the dominant mode in three of Zingg's four recording situations; it rests on one source. Near buildings and trees the calls look like serotine calls. The middle shape point is Zingg's frequency at mid-call; the 0.2 point is a drawing choice.

notes: Search calls are a steep FM sweep into a long shallow tail near 22 to 25 kHz. Duration, end and peak frequency are Funakoshi's (2010) search-phase calls of 10 bats at feeding areas in Kyushu. Fukui et al. (2004) recorded 21 bats leaving roosts in Hokkaido under the older name Vespertilio superans: 6.2 ms (2.3 to 19.9), start 48.1 kHz, end 21.8 kHz, peak 24.2 kHz. The Handbook of the Mammals of the World says the species was formerly called V. superans. Start frequency is from Fukui et al. (2004) only and comes from bats leaving roosts, so a search call probably starts lower. The Handbook gives a peak of about 30.8 kHz with frequencies from 22.8 to 46 kHz for typical pulses. Calls on leaving a roost are shorter (3.2 ms in Kyushu) and usually show a second harmonic (Funakoshi 2010). No opened source gives a start-to-start interval for search calls. The noctule (Nyctalus aviator) calls lower and longer.
